learn.title: Pseudo-clefts with What
learn.html:
A cleft sentence (cleft sentence) splits a simple sentence into two parts to place the focus of information at the end, where English naturally puts the most important information. The most common type is the pseudo-cleft with what: the clause introduced by what works as the subject, be acts as the hinge and the emphasised element comes last.

Neutral sentenceCleft sentence
I miss the market most.What I miss most is the market.
The noise annoys me.What annoys me is the noise.
We need a better bus service.What we need is a better bus service.
I regret selling the house.What I regret is selling the house. / What I regret is that I sold the house.

Important points:

  • Verb in the clause and be. When the emphasised element is a verb, the pattern repeats the action: What she did was (to) apply for a transfer. The to is optional if did appears in the clause (What I did was call him = What I did was to call him).
  • Clause as complement. After be you can use a noun, a gerund, an infinitive or a clause with that: What worries me is how fast prices are rising.
  • Inverted version (reverse pseudo-cleft). The order can be reversed for a more conversational, concluding tone: The market is what I miss most. / That's what I can't stand. Here the focus goes to the beginning.
  • Agreement. With singular is it is acceptable even when what follows is plural (What we need is more parks); in very careful register you may see What the city needs are affordable homes, but is is always safe.
  • Do not repeat the pronoun. In Spanish you might say «lo que me gusta es eso»; in English the clause with what already contains the object, so do not add it: What I like is the view (not What I like it is the view).

Register: it works in both speech and formal writing; it can introduce a conclusion (What this study shows is…) or soften a complaint (What I'd say is that it's a bit pricey).

watch.wrong: What I like it is the view from the balcony.
watch.right: What I like is the view from the balcony.
watch.why: The what-clause already contains the object: do not add it (a calque of «lo que me gusta es…»).

watch.wrong: What annoys me it is the noise.
watch.right: What annoys me is the noise.
watch.why: After the what-clause comes be directly; do not repeat the subject with it.

watch.wrong: The thing what bothers me is the traffic.
watch.right: The thing that bothers me is the traffic.
watch.why: After the thing, use that (or nothing), never what: what already includes «the thing that».

watch.wrong: What I did was to went to the agency.
watch.right: What I did was go to the agency.
watch.why: After What I did was comes the infinitive, with or without to, never a conjugated verb form.

learn.title: It-clefts: It was … that …
learn.html:
The it-cleft follows the pattern It + be + emphasised element + that/who + rest. Unlike the pseudo-cleft, the focus appears in the middle and is mainly used to correct, contrast or identify someone or something specific.

Emphasised elementExample
Subject (person)It was my landlord who/that raised the rent.
Subject (thing)It was the rent that made us leave.
ObjectIt's the noise that I can't stand.
Place / time complementIt was in 2019 that the market closed. / It was on this street that we met.
With a time negationIt wasn't until I left home that I learned to cook.

Details that distinguish the advanced level:

  • who / that / which. With people use who or that; with things, that (which is possible but more formal). With time or place complements, use that; when and where appear in speech but are considered informal in formal writing.
  • Pronouns. In informal speech the object form is used: It was him who found the flat. In very formal writing you may hear It was he who…, but it sounds stilted.
  • Agreement in the second part. If the focus is I, careful English makes the verb agree with it: It was I who was late; in everyday speech: It was me who was late.
  • Tense of be. It is… that for present facts; It was… that for the past. With modals: It might have been the rent that decided it.
  • Questions. You can ask about the focus: Was it the price that put you off?
  • It is not a passive. Compare: The developers demolished the market / The market was demolished by the developers / It was the developers who demolished the market (here what is emphasised is who did it).

Contrast with Spanish: Spanish does the same with fue… quien/el que/lo que… («fue mi casero quien subió la renta»), but English does not allow omitting that/who when the focus is the subject: you cannot say It was my landlord raised the rent.

watch.wrong: It was my landlord raised the rent.
watch.right: It was my landlord who raised the rent.
watch.why: When the focus is the subject, who/that is obligatory; it can be omitted only if the focus is an object (It was the flat I wanted).

watch.wrong: It was in 2019 what they demolished the market.
watch.right: It was in 2019 that they demolished the market.
watch.why: What cannot act as a connector in an it-cleft; use that.

watch.wrong: It was not until I moved out when I realised.
watch.right: It was not until I moved out that I realised.
watch.why: It was not until… is followed by that, not when.

watch.wrong: Is the price what put you off?
watch.right: Was it the price that put you off?
watch.why: The question keeps the structure: Was it + focus + that + rest.

learn.title: Emphasis with do / does / did
learn.html:
In affirmative sentences the auxiliary do does not normally appear, but it can be inserted as an emphatic device. Use do/does in the present and did in the past, followed by the base form of the verb (the auxiliary already carries the tense and person).

NeutralEmphatic (stress on do/does/did)
I like this flat.I do like this flat.
She lives alone.She does live alone.
They warned us.They did warn us.
Be careful with the lease.Do be careful with the lease.

What it is for (and what nuance it adds):

  • Contradicting or correcting a doubt from the listener: — You never call. — I did call! I called on Sunday.
  • Conceding something before qualifying it: I do like living here; it's just that the commute is exhausting. This is a very natural pattern in conversation for introducing a but.
  • Intensifying a wish or politeness: Do come in! / Do sit down. The imperative with do sounds warm, almost insistent; in tense contexts it can sound impatient (Do be quiet!).
  • Confirming that something is indeed true after an expectation to the contrary: The area does have a bad reputation, but it has improved.

Formal rules: (1) it never combines with another auxiliary: I do have, but not I do can; with modals you stress the modal with your voice (I CAN help). (2) The main verb goes in the base form, without -s or -ed: She does like, he did warn. (3) In writing it is marked with italics or, more soberly, with adverbs such as certainly, indeed, really; overusing emphatic do in an academic text sounds too colloquial.

Spanish vs. English: in Spanish we mark this with «sí» («sí me gusta», «sí te avisé»). English has no such particle: do/did fulfils that function.

watch.why: After does/did the verb takes the base form: the -s is already on does.

watch.wrong: I did went to the meeting.
watch.right: I did go to the meeting.
watch.why: After did comes the infinitive without to; the past is already marked by did.

watch.wrong: I do can see the problem.
watch.right: I can see the problem. (con acento en can)
watch.why: Emphatic do does not combine with modals; the modal is stressed with the voice instead.

watch.wrong: Yes, I am like it very much.
watch.right: Yes, I do like it very much.
watch.why: Emphasis is not made with be + verb: insert do before the base verb.

learn.title: Other clefts: All, The thing, The reason, The place
learn.html:
Besides what there is a family of structures that change what is emphasised and how much the message is softened or concluded. All follow the pattern clause + be + focus.

StructureExampleNuance
All (that) + subject + verb + beAll I wanted was a quiet place.Downplays: 'the only thing that…'.
The thing (that)… + beThe thing that bothers me is the traffic.Conversational; very frequent.
The reason (why/that)… + be thatThe reason why we left was that rents kept rising.Cause; why is optional.
The place where… + beThe place where I feel most at home is my grandmother's kitchen.Place; evokes emotion.
The first/last/only thing… + beThe first thing we noticed was the smell of bread.Sequence: focus on the first or last element.
What happened/follows is (that)…What happened was that the landlord sold the building.Narrative; anticipates a twist.

Fine points:

  • The reason is that, not because. After The reason… is comes that: The reason is that we couldn't afford it; The reason is because… is common in spoken English, but it is considered incorrect in formal writing and in exams such as the TOEFL.
  • All + did + was + base (with or without to). All she did was ask for a quieter room. With did in the clause, the to is usually omitted; in other cases it is kept (All I want is to sleep).
  • The place where / the day when / the way (that). The way she explained it was clear (not the way how).
  • When not to use them. Too many clefts make a text heavy. Use them once or twice per paragraph to highlight the key idea; for the rest, use normal word order.
  • Comparing focus. What I like is the view (what), It's the view that I like (contrast: the view, not something else) and I do like the view (emphatic affirmation of the verb): each one puts the stress in a different place.

watch.wrong: The reason why I left is because the rent was too high.
watch.right: The reason why I left is that the rent was too high.
watch.why: After The reason… is comes that; is because is avoided in formal register.

watch.wrong: All she did was asked for a quieter room.
watch.right: All she did was ask for a quieter room.
watch.why: After All she did was comes the infinitive (with or without to), never the past.

watch.wrong: The way how he explained it was clear.
watch.right: The way he explained it was clear.
watch.why: The way does not take how: it is used alone (or with that).

watch.wrong: The place that I grew up has changed.
watch.right: The place where I grew up has changed.
watch.why: If the relative clause expresses place (grew up in/at), where is needed.

learn.title: Emphasising and qualifying opinions
learn.html:
• What strikes me is… / What I find remarkable is… — introduce a personal observation with emphasis.
  • It's not so much X as Y. — meaning «it is not so much X as Y»: It's not so much the rent as the lack of services.
  • If anything,… — qualify or correct cautiously: If anything, the area has got noisier.
  • I do see your point, but… — concede before disagreeing.
  • The point is (that)… / The thing is (that)… — get to the heart of the matter in a conversational way.
  • To be fair,… / In fairness,… — soften a criticism.
  • That's precisely what I mean. / That's exactly why… — reinforce an argument.
  • Admittedly,… / Granted,… — acknowledge a point against you.
  • All things considered,… — close with an overall assessment.

What strikes me most about my neighbourhood is how quiet it has become. When I was a child, the streets were never silent: children played football beside the market, and neighbours chatted from their balconies until midnight. What I remember best is the smell of bread from the bakery on the corner, which closed three years ago.

It was in the early 2010s that things began to change. It was the arrival of short-term holiday flats that transformed the area most, and it is the long-standing residents who have borne the cost. What many families can no longer afford is the rent, which has doubled in a decade. It is not so much that the neighbourhood has become dangerous as that it has become unaffordable.

To be fair, there have been gains. Amenities have improved, the pavements are cleaner, and the new cafés do give the area a lively, cosmopolitan feel. I do appreciate the cycle lanes, which make my commute far more pleasant. Admittedly, a trendy, well-connected district is hard to resist.

If anything, though, the benefits are unevenly shared. The people who gain most are property owners and visitors, while elderly tenants and young families are slowly being pushed out. What worries me is that a neighbourhood with no affordable housing loses its character, becoming a showcase rather than a community.

What I would like to see is a more balanced approach: a cap on tourist lets and genuine investment in affordable housing. A vibrant, gentrifying neighbourhood is not necessarily a better one, and the old baker would, I think, agree.

write.prompt: Write a formal letter of 280 to 350 words to the city council about rising rents and the lack of affordable housing in your city. Describe the problem, state the causes clearly (It is… that…, The reason… is that…) and propose three concrete solutions. Keep a firm but polite tone and avoid overusing colloquial emphatic do.
checklist: Formal greeting and closing
Clear description of the problem with data or examples
At least three varied clefts (What, It, The reason…)
The reason… is that (no because)
Three concrete proposals using housing vocabulary
Polite but firm tone (If anything, To be fair, Admittedly)
Between 280 and 350 words
write.model:
Dear Members of the Council,

I am writing to express my deep concern about rising rents and the shortage of affordable housing in our city, which now threaten the stability of thousands of households.

According to the latest figures from the municipal housing office, average rents have risen by almost forty per cent in the past six years, while wages have grown by less than ten. A young teacher in my own street, for instance, now spends more than sixty per cent of her salary on a one-bedroom flat. What is particularly worrying is that many residents are being forced to leave the neighbourhoods in which they have lived all their lives.

The causes are not difficult to identify. It is the conversion of residential flats into tourist accommodation that has reduced the supply of long-term rentals most sharply. The main reason rents continue to climb is that new construction has focused almost exclusively on luxury developments. Admittedly, investment is welcome and, to be fair, the council has taken some steps in the right direction. Nevertheless, these measures have been too limited to make a real difference.

I would therefore respectfully urge the council to consider three measures. First, a strict limit should be placed on the number of licences granted for short-term tourist lets. Second, a proportion of every new development, say thirty per cent, ought to be reserved for affordable housing. Third, the council should create a public rental scheme, offering stable contracts to young people and families on moderate incomes.

All that is required is the political will to act. If anything, delay will only make the problem more expensive to solve. I would be grateful for the opportunity to discuss these proposals at a public meeting, and I trust that you will give them serious consideration.

Yours faithfully,

Marta Delgado

reading.title: The street that changed
reading.intro: Read this personal essay about a neighbourhood in transformation and answer the questions.
paragraphs: When I left Calle Naranjo at nineteen, it was a street that smelled of frying onions and diesel. Twenty years on, what greets me at the corner is a cold-brew bar with a neon sign in English. It would be easy to write a lament, and I have read plenty of them. But what interests me is not nostalgia; it is the question of who gets to decide what a neighbourhood is for.

My aunt Lupe still lives in the building where I grew up, though not for much longer. It was last spring that her landlord told her the rent would almost double. 'It isn't that I mind the new neighbours,' she told me, stirring her coffee with unusual force. 'What I mind is being treated as though I were part of the scenery.' She has lived in that third-floor flat for thirty-one years, long enough to have watched the pharmacy become a phone shop, then a gallery, and now a studio that sells ceramic cups for the price of a week's groceries.

The usual word for all this is gentrification, and it is a word that is easy to overuse. Developers speak of regeneration; residents speak of displacement; economists, characteristically, speak of neighbourhood sorting. Each of them is describing something real. Nobody disputes that the street is safer, cleaner and better lit than it was. What is disputed is who has been paid for those improvements, and who has paid for them. Property values have tripled in a decade, yet the typical household income on the street has barely risen. The people who can afford to stay are largely those who bought early or inherited; everyone else has moved to the outskirts, where a cheaper flat comes with a commute of two hours each way.

That commute is, I think, the part of the story that gets least attention. It was only when I spent a week travelling with Lupe's former neighbour, Mauricio, that I understood it. He now lives on a sprawling estate at the edge of the city, where rows of identical houses stand without a single shop, clinic or café within walking distance. He leaves at five in the morning and returns after eight at night. 'I do have a bigger kitchen,' he said with a tired smile, 'but I hardly ever see it in daylight.' The amenities the rest of us take for granted, such as a pharmacy round the corner or a school one can walk to, are exactly what he traded away for space.

None of this means that change itself is the enemy. A street that never changes is a museum, and nobody has ever wanted to pay rent in a museum. The real issue is pace and participation. The cities that have handled the problem best tend to do three things: they cap sudden rent increases, they require developers to set aside a share of every new building as affordable housing, and, hardest of all, they consult the people who already live there before the cranes arrive. None of these measures is glamorous, and none is cheap.

On my last evening, Lupe took me up to the roof. The city was doing what it does at dusk: the lights came on in waves, a dog barked somewhere, and a vendor's whistle drifted up from the street below. 'You see?' she said. 'It's the sounds that haven't changed.' I thought about that on the flight home. Perhaps what makes a place feel like home is less the buildings than the small, unremarkable routines that survive inside them, and it is precisely those routines that money finds hardest to protect.

listening.title: Viewing a flat
listening.intro: Listen to a couple viewing a flat with the estate agent. You can play it again.

lines.text: Right, so this is the living area. As you can see, it's open-plan, and the windows face south, so you get sun most of the afternoon.
It's lovely, honestly. What strikes me is how much light there is. The photos didn't do it justice.
It is bright. What I'm wondering about is the street, though. Is it noisy at night?
Not at all. It's one of the quietest roads in the area. There's a bar at the far end, but it closes at eleven.
Hm. And the commute? We both work downtown.
It's about twenty-five minutes by metro. The station is a five-minute walk, and it was the new line that made this neighbourhood so sought-after.
It's a bit above our budget, though. We did say nothing over fourteen thousand a month.
I understand. The landlord is asking sixteen, but there may be room to negotiate, particularly if you're willing to sign for two years.
Two years is a big commitment. All I'd want is a clause allowing us to leave after twelve months if our jobs change.
That's not unusual. I'll raise it with him. What you need to bear in mind is that another couple is coming to view it at five.
Ah, so that's a bit of pressure, then.
Not pressure, just reality. It's a popular street.
Let's talk it over outside. It was the kitchen that worried me, honestly. It's rather cramped.
I know, but I do think we could live with it. It's the location that sells it for me.

tasks.model: I grew up in a leafy suburb on the edge of Puebla. It was a tranquil place, with wide pavements and old jacaranda trees. What I miss most is the sense of community: the neighbours knew each other by name. It was the tianguis on Sundays that really brought the street to life. Nowadays it's a lot busier, and honestly, what worries me is how many of the old houses have been replaced by apartment blocks.

Admittedly, though, it's not so much the improvement that bothers me as the way it prices out long-term residents. What cities need is a mix of measures: rent caps, affordable housing quotas and a say for residents. The reason it works badly in many places is that decisions are taken before anyone asks the neighbours.
